segments.text: Azure Migrate helps customers understand and modernize their on-premises estate. In the AI era, we have an opportunity to extend that journey. Not only helping customers decide how to move an application to Azure, but also helping them identify where AI can create meaningful value, and what it would take to deliver that value responsibly.

Azure Migrate begins with discovery. It prepares an inventory of virtual machines, web applications, databases, file shares, containers, and supporting dependencies. Customers can then organize these components as a complete application, a unit that works and moves together. Assessment maps each component to an appropriate Azure target. A web application might map to Azure App Service. SQL Server might map to Azure SQL Managed Instance. A containerized workload might map to Azure Kubernetes Service. This gives us rich application intelligence: the application boundary, runtime, dependencies, assessed targets, readiness, and cost context.

That assessment is excellent at answering the cloud-era question: where and how should this application run in Azure? But customers increasingly ask a second question: how can I use AI in this existing application? And, if I already use AI on-premises, how should I modernize that capability in Azure? This leads to two strategic questions. How do we help customers find credible AI opportunities in the applications they already own? And what should the next generation of Azure Migrate look like in the AI era?

The proposed idea is an AI Feasibility Assessment as a new step in the Azure Migrate journey. Discover. Assess. AI Feasibility Assessment. Design. Estimate. Modernize. It adds an AI modernization layer on top of existing application intelligence. The goal is not to turn every application into an AI project. The goal is to identify which application and workflow combinations justify a bounded experiment, which need remediation first, and which should not pursue AI.

For each selected application, the assessment should answer four practical questions. Where can AI create meaningful business or engineering value? Is the application and its data technically ready for that scenario? Which integrations, Azure services, and security or governance controls are required? And what is the pragmatic path from proof of concept, to pilot, to production? The output is a reviewable decision pack with explicit evidence gaps and production gates, not a generic list of AI ideas.

The experience combines two evidence streams. Azure Migrate contributes observed application facts: components, dependencies, runtime, assessed targets, and migration findings. The customer contributes the business meaning: the process to improve, users, desired outcome, data constraints, compliance needs, and expected usage. The assessment then produces a feasibility summary, data and integration readiness, governance considerations, recommended Azure AI services, indicative cost scenarios, an AI-ready architecture extension, and a proof of concept roadmap. The key design principle is explainability. Observed facts, customer-provided context, inferred assumptions, and missing evidence remain visibly separate. Rules and deterministic calculations control the decision pack. Generative AI can improve the narrative, but it does not silently invent readiness or cost.

Let’s see the proposed experience in the Azure Migrate simulator. Discovery and assessment are already complete. We will start with the B P T co application, inspect its current Azure architecture, capture a document-processing outcome, generate an AI Feasibility Assessment, and then see exactly where the proposed AI services fit in the application landing zone.

Discovery and assessment are already complete, so we move directly to Plan. Under Plan, Application Groups brings related infrastructure and workloads together as one application. B P T co includes its virtual machines and the discovered web, database, container, orchestration, and file-share components that belong to the application boundary. This is the scope we carry forward. AI feasibility is not assessed against an isolated server. It is assessed against the complete application and a customer-confirmed workflow.

First, we look at the current proposed Azure architecture with AI turned off. This is the application landing-zone view produced from the migration assessment. It shows secure ingress, network boundaries, shared platform services, assessed application targets, and data or storage dependencies. At this point, the design answers where and how B P T co could run in Azure. It does not yet add an AI capability.

Now the customer wants to explore an AI opportunity for the same application. In Decide, the Assessment experience includes AI Feasibility Assessment. We select B P T co, then choose the broad solution idea: Document Processing and Enrichment. These categories guide the assessment; they do not predetermine a service purchase or claim that the scenario is feasible.

The customer now supplies the context discovery cannot infer. Here the process is document intake and enrichment across invoices, contracts, and attachments. The intended capability is classification, field extraction, metadata enrichment, summarization, business-rule validation, and human review for exceptions. The business outcome is explicit: reduce manual data entry by sixty percent, reduce processing time by fifty percent, and target ninety-five percent accuracy for critical fields, while keeping controlled access, approval, and auditability.

The customer has confirmed the processing boundary. The entered intent, expected outcome, a deterministic local draft, and minimized evidence labels may be sent to the configured Foundry model. Uploaded content is treated as data, not as instructions. The result is a versioned decision pack. It separates business fit, data readiness, integration readiness, security and governance, delivery and operations, and economics. For this scenario, the proposed capability set includes Azure AI Document Intelligence for extraction and classification, Azure AI Search for permission-aware retrieval, a Microsoft Foundry model for grounded enrichment and summarization, workflow orchestration, approved storage, and monitoring. The estimate is shown as low, base, and high scenarios with explicit assumptions and a reserve. The output also identifies evidence gaps and defines the smallest bounded proof of concept and the tests required before any production decision. A proof of concept candidate means justified experimentation, not production readiness.

From the assessment we move directly into the AI-ready architecture. The original application design is preserved, but the diagram is replaced with a reviewed AI-ready variant for this application. The new capability extension shows where document intelligence, search, model access, orchestration, approved storage, and observability fit alongside the assessed application and data services. Every AI node is visibly marked as proposed. The diagram links back to the exact assessment revision, and base application cost remains separate from the incremental AI planning budget. If the checkbox is turned off, the architecture returns to the original migration design. AI is an explicit, assessed extension, not a silent default.

This demonstration connects four things that are usually separated. It reuses existing application intelligence. It captures the customer’s business intent and outcome. It produces an explainable, evidence-backed decision pack. And it carries the approved scenario into an AI-ready architecture without losing the base application design. The result is a qualified modernization conversation and a practical handoff, not a generic AI brainstorm.

The larger vision is simple. Azure Migrate has traditionally helped answer: how do I move this application to Azure? In the AI era, it can also help answer: how can I transform this application with AI, and what would it take to get there? Migration remains the foundation. AI Feasibility adds the next modernization decision at exactly the point where the customer already understands the application and is choosing its future.

Azure Migrate already works through a broad ecosystem, including C M F, S A Desk, cloud solution architects, systems integrators, and other delivery partners. AI Feasibility can extend those relationships with a better-qualified application opportunity and a versioned handoff. It can also create new collaboration paths with Microsoft Foundry, Azure Frontier, AI field engineers, and Forward Deployed Engineers. Azure Migrate owns the application-to-opportunity decision experience. Platform and delivery teams validate and build the solution. The customer retains ownership of business value, data authorization, and production acceptance. The next step is a bounded design-partner validation: human-reviewed recommendations, clear evidence gates, and measurable movement from qualified opportunity to customer-owned proof of concept. Azure Migrate helps us understand the application. AI Feasibility helps the customer decide how that application can create new value in the AI era.
